blocks.1: Farming has from of old been the most important livelihood here. In Fonnevika there was a coaching inn, and there was a general store from around the mid-1850s. The store also sold wine and beer. Here too, as mentioned, came the first steamship agency in the area, when Fylkesbaatane started operating. For some 10–12 years a margarine factory was also run there, started by Fredrik Larsen. The factory is said to have been called “Stjernen” (the Star); it was later moved to Bergen. For a time the merchants in Fonnevika handled the post for Eivindvik sub-post office. There was also a small dye works in Fonnevika. It was owned by a man called Nedrål, and it was bought by Peder Rasmussen Sandal, who started something called a “packet dye factory”. In 1892 he moved over to the mainland and started the business that is now P.R. Sandal A/S.
blocks.2: The smith Søren Larsen also had his business in Fonnevik before he moved over to the mainland. The permanent school that Dahl ran in Fonnevika was moved to Undertun when the schoolhouse came there in 1835. Fonnevik has been used as a place for court sittings (ting). Statistics show that 25 people lived in Fonnevika in 1875.
blocks.3: The place has also been called Svinevik (pig bay). That name apparently came from the priests keeping pigs “grazing” there in older times. For a long time Fonnevik was home to parish clerks and curates.
blocks.4: East of Magnar Sognnes's holding, down by the shore, a “hole” into the rock can be seen. An attempt was made to mine copper there. The place is still called “Kopargruva” (the copper mine).
blocks.5: A bakery has also been run in Fonnevika. Lars Nygård says his father, Johannes Nygård, was a baker there.
blocks.6: In the local history Ivar Kleiva has included a good deal about Fonnevika, its people and the businesses there.
blocks.7: The well-known master builder Anders Korsvold lived in Fonna. Among much else he built Kvikne's Hotel in Balestrand, Mundal Hotel in Fjærland and Maristova in the mountains above Lærdal. He was called “the church builder” and was master builder for Mjømna church and the English church in Balestrand, among others. It was also he who built the old parsonage here in Eivindvik in 1902. His son, Ola Korsvold, became a master painter. It was he who did the painting when the church was renovated in 1938.
blocks.8: At the end of the 1800s, probably in 1870–80, Jon Sundal, at Midtun, farm no. 20, holding no. 3, ran a fulling mill by the river at Indrebøen. The walls of the fulling mill stood until a few years ago. Sundalskaia (the Sundal quay) is named after “Sundalen”; he had his boathouse where the quay lies.
blocks.9: Kahrsbua was another well-known boathouse. It stood where “the new bridge” crosses over to Undertun. It was customary to put up notices on its door about meetings and parties and other things to be announced. It was named after “Kahrsen”, who lived at Gryta, holding no. 3.
blocks.10: For a time there were three tailors in the village. Olav Nese from Arnafjord came here in 1910, bought farm no. 21, holding no. 4, and ran a tailor's workshop on the first floor of the house until after the war of 40–45. He died in 1947. He also cut hair; indeed, it was so common to go to the tailor for a haircut that a little schoolgirl telling about Harald Fairhair said that when he had finally united Norway into one kingdom, “he went to the tailor and had his hair cut.”
blocks.11: Eilev Buene, from Frønningen, came to Eivindvik in 1929. He too worked as a tailor and lived in various places here (I know he lived at Indre Midtun, holding no. 1, and at Undertun, holding no. 1). He died in the 1960s.
blocks.12: Jørna Midthun, in Prestneset, was a trained tailor. She did a fair amount of sewing; among other things she made many men's suits. She was born in Fusa and married to Nicolay Midthun. Nicolay was, as mentioned earlier, a particularly skilled drill smith and was often away on construction work, but he also helped many with various smithing jobs in the forge he had on his smallholding. Jørna and Nicolay's house is very old. It is said to have been moved here as a tenant's house on the so-called “Småpakta” (small lease) on the parsonage land, probably about 170–180 years ago. This house, only about 8 x 6 m, with 1 ½ storeys, was often used as “lodgings” for overnight guests. In addition to their own family there could often be 8–10 people staying the night. Most of the guests were people attending public meetings – meetings in those days often lasted for days, the tax assessment committee's meetings for weeks – but also churchgoers, for example at confirmations, which then lasted two days, and patients the doctor wanted to keep an eye on for a while got rooms in the house. All the overnight guests had full board. Jørna was often alone in running the house and smallholding, and with many guests in the house and at the table, on top of looking after children and the animals on the holding, she surely had her hands full, but still found time for sewing. Talk about willingness to work and about room in the heart and in the house!
blocks.13: In 1927 Ola Midthun started a shop at “Stranda”, below Haugane, facing Midtunvågen. In 1974 the shop, together with the property Ola and his wife Helga had built up there, was sold to Irma and Svein Høyland, who moved here from Ikjefjord. After both had found other work in the village, they stopped running the shop and let the shop premises to others, but since the turn of the year 1990–91 there has been no trade there. A quay with a goods shed was built by the sea, and for many years Fylkesbaatane had a stop there to deliver goods to the shop. In the timetables the stop is called “Midtunvåg”. In everyday speech the shop was called “Småmagasinet” (the little store). This name surely came from the shop having been started in a small boathouse.
blocks.14: Toralf Sande was a master smith and ran an engineering workshop in Eivindvik, on leasehold no. 9, from 1929 to 1956. He was a skilled craftsman of great use to farmers, fishermen and others who needed his help. He was also a good gunsmith.
blocks.15: In 1938 Ragnhild and Jørgen Midtun opened a nursing home for the mentally ill on their farm, farm no. 20, holding no. 1. This home had room for 12–13 patients and was run for about 25 years.
blocks.16: Eivindvik Slipp og Mek. verkstad. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.17: Eivindvik Slipp og Mek. Verkstad (slipway and engineering works) came in 1954. It was Lars Nygård who started it, and after a short time his son, Johannes Nygård, came home and took over. He had earlier worked as a mechanic at Jørpeland on Jæren. For many years they ran an ordinary repair yard for boats, but later went over to building quays, which is their main business today. They have become specialists in such work and have had many contracts, both large and small, all over Western Norway. In 1992 they did some restoration work on the veteran boat “Stavenes”, one of Fylkesbaatane's old passenger boats. “Stavenes” has been bought back from England by a partnership to be restored as she was when she sailed the routes here.
blocks.18: In the house up on “the farm” at Haugane lived Ole Ellingsen, who did shoe repairs. I do not know when he came here and started as a shoemaker. He died in 1945.
blocks.19: The shop at Haugane. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.20: Karen Midtun (farm no. 19, holding no. 2) and Georg Guttormsen (from Torvund), who married in 1912, leased a site at Haugane, built a house there and ran a general store in the cellar until 1925. Then they moved away. The house was sold, pulled down and put up again in Virkesdal.
blocks.21: Guttorm Arnesen settled in Eivindvik and started a shoemaker's workshop in 1935–36. At first he worked for a short time on the farm his wife Helga came from (Henriksbø, farm no. 21, holding no. 1), but he built a house on leasehold no. 11 on the parsonage land and had his workshop in the cellar there. He ran the workshop into the 1970s, when he had to stop for health reasons.
blocks.22: In the cellar of the house at farm no. 15, holding no. 22, Ivar Mongstad and Halvor Vatne started a joinery workshop right after the war (1940–45). For health reasons Vatne withdrew from the business, and in 1947 Mongstad bought farm no. 15, holding no. 23, put up a new factory building there and ran Eivindvik Snikkarverkstad (joinery) for many years (I think about 20). The production was mostly windows and doors.
blocks.23: The business “Wevling og Opdal”, Erling Wevling and Martin Opdal, started in Wevling's cellar, farm no. 22, holding no. 5, in 1949. It too was a joinery; they produced glazing, doors and stairs. In 1958 they dissolved the partnership; Wevling continued in his cellar, and Opdal started the firm “M. Opdal” in his own house, farm no. 22, holding no. 8. Later, in the 1960s, he bought a site at farm no. 22, holding no. 3, and built a new workshop there. Opdal was an exceptionally able stair maker. Many homes have fine handcrafted items by Wevling, such as small wooden containers, boxes, mats and much more.
blocks.24: Another who has created many fine things is the district doctor Tom Bache-Wiig. He came here at the end of 1969. As mentioned elsewhere in this booklet, he did a great deal for patient transport and local boat services in the municipality. He is also active in many other fields; among other things he is a skilled graphic artist and painter who has had exhibitions both in Norway and abroad. He started the band “Epidemic” and was an active musician for many years. On top of all this he also finds time to design and make various types of knives. He makes every part of the knives himself, and they sell well both in Norway and in several other countries.
blocks.25: In 1967 the farmers at Midtun set up a shared sawmill, which has been, and still is, of great use to themselves and also to others in the area who need timber now and then.
blocks.26: From 1947 Ole J. Midtun had a somewhat smaller sawmill in his barn.
blocks.27: Bernt and Aslaug Stendal came to Eivindvik and built a house here in 1962. Bernt was employed at Eivindvik Slipp og Mek. verkstad. He is very handy and good at many things. In the cellar of his house he fitted out his own well-equipped private workshop, where, even after he retired and left “the Slipway”, he did people many good turns.
blocks.28: The first taxi licence in Eivindvik went to Birger Flolid in 1964.
blocks.29: In addition to the work on the farms, people have from of old done some fishing and had some seasonal work during the great fisheries, such as the herring fishery. As road building, hydropower development and other construction picked up, many also worked on construction sites and in building. Something the people of Gulen early became known for was their skill as telephone workers. In Sørfjorden in Hardanger I once heard it said that when difficult lines were to be built, it took men from Gulen. Almost all men in Gulen had at some time, at least for periods, worked on telephone lines. It was very interesting to listen when the old-timers got together and refreshed their memories of the time “on the telephone”.
blocks.30: Around 1906–07 it seems that many from here went to Iceland to work on telephone lines. In “Fremad” for 13 January 1907 I find the first travel letter from Iceland. It is signed Hans Mikkelsen. Who that was, or whether it was just an assumed name, I have not found out.
blocks.31: The retired telephone employee Oddkjell Bosheim, Lærdal, has researched the work of the telegraph administration. He says that Otto L. Midthun, farm no. 20, holding no. 1, was much involved in planning the building of the telephone network both in Northern Norway and in Iceland, but I have not heard or seen anywhere that Otto himself was in Iceland. Three of his sons were there, however, and it was one of them, Nicolay Midthun, who among other things was in charge of building the first telephone line in Iceland. It was near Akureyri. For his work in Iceland he received the Icelandic Order of the Falcon. Nicolay later became director of Moss Telefonanlegg. This is said to have been one of the last private telephone companies in the country to be taken over by the Telegraph Administration. Nicolay also received the King's Medal of Merit in gold.
blocks.32: M. Midtun in front of the memorial in Gular raised by telephone workers from Gulen. Photo: Ottar Midtun.
blocks.33: In Gaular there stands a long, narrow stone used as a telephone pole. It was raised by Otto Midthun and his crew in 1892. The stone was straightened in 1990, and a centenary ceremony was held at the stone in 1992; it now bears a memorial plaque. The letters O.M., H.U. and apparently also H.H. are carved into the stone. This stone will be mentioned in Ingemar Nordstrand's book on the postal road between Bergen and Trondheim, for which he is now gathering material. Nordstrand says that Otto Midthun was the first telegraph manager in Sogn og Fjordane. Otto was also active in the village societies when he was at home, perhaps especially as a singer and in the work with the choir. He helped start Gulen Sparebank and was also mayor of the municipality for a short time.
blocks.34: Some from here also emigrated to America. A few came back, but most became Americans.
blocks.35: Some made their living as seamen, and, as mentioned, some of them settled here because Eivindvik had so much transhipment traffic; the boats often lay here, and it was easy to get to and from. Some extra jobs also came from ferry-boat services. Of people who ran their own somewhat larger freight boats, we had Albert and Jørgen Sognnes with M/K “Sognnes”, M/B “Vatløy”, owned by Artur Søreide and Harald Nikøy, “Balder I”, owned by Olav Midthun, and M/B “Grindheimsvåg”, owned by Ingolf Kyrkjeøy.
blocks.36: In recent times the business of Per Vold, who owns and runs several smaller passenger boats, has provided jobs. He operates both charter trips and scheduled services (village and school routes for the municipality and a local route for FSF).
blocks.37: Eivindvik Hotel, formerly Eivindvik Vertshus (the inn), came with its jobs in 1979. At about the same time Steinar Jørs started his plumbing firm here. He bought the old bank building. The bank had then got its new building on the same site where the inn and Eivindvik sosialsenter (the social centre) put up their buildings. The doctor's surgery, the national insurance office, the social services and the sheriff's office moved into the social centre's premises.
blocks.38: The newspaper “Bygdebladet” published its first issue on 20 June 1985. The editorial office and printing works were on the first floor of the bank building. The publisher and editor was Oleiv Gjetle, formerly head of social services in Gulen. Unfortunately the paper closed after a short time.
blocks.39: Grete and Kjell Solheim ran a photography business for about 6 years from 1979. For the first 3 years they too were on the first floor of the bank building (the rooms where Gulen Rekneskapskontor, the accounting office, is now), and then, for about 3 years, they rented premises in the cellar of Irma and Svein Høyland's house (farm no. 15, holding no. 27). The firm was called G-Foto. It was sold to Hans Petter Martiniussen on Byrknesøy, who ran it for some years under the name Gulen Fotosenter.
blocks.40: Marta Sandal ran a hairdressing salon in Eivindvik from 1958 to 1967 and from 1981 to 1985. For the first 5 years she had the salon in the house of her father, the head of schools Søren Randal (farm no. 15, holding no. 26), and then for 4 years in her own house until she and her husband, Per Sandal, moved away in 1967. When they came back and took over the business P.R. Sandal A/S in 1980, she reopened the salon on the first floor of the business building on the quay (1981) and ran it until 1985.
blocks.41: On 25 March 1996 Borgny Solbakk and Oddny Sognefest started the firm Eivindvik Husflid. They rent premises in one of the buildings of Eivindvik Sosialsenter I/S. The firm sells handicrafts and souvenirs. Oddny later withdrew from the firm, and Borgny runs the business on her own.
blocks.42: The new growth industry, fish farming, was extensive in Gulen in the 1980s. Here in Eivindvik Olav Bøe started trout farming in the sea below his house. The business was later expanded, turned into a limited company called Gullaks A/S, and moved to Stafsneset, where a quay and an operations building were built. In the early 1990s the facility was taken over by Eivindvik Fiskeoppdrett and sold on to Firda Havbruk A/S in 1996.
blocks.43: Cod farming was also tried, but at that time it proved very difficult to get fry for the farms, so this branch of fish farming has not yet become extensive. An attempt was made in Fonna. Kåre Håvåg was behind it; the firm was called Fonna Fisk A/S.
blocks.44: In the 1930s and 40s the big herring came regularly in to the coast of Western Norway in winter, and many then took part in fishing and herring work. The fishing was mostly done with beach seines. There was good fishing among the islands in Solund and Gulen too. Those doing herring work went mostly to Florø, but also to other places with herring reception.
blocks.45: Carrying herring was important employment for many who had suitable boats. The brothers Albert and Jørgen Sognnes (at Fagerbakken in Fonnevika) ran such a business with M/K “Sognnes”. The herring had to be scooped up by hand in those days, so there were surely many hard shifts getting it from the seine to the boat and from the boat up onto the reception quay. Days and nights could go by without the dockers (the workers on quays and sites) getting proper sleep. Everyone worked flat out in the hectic “herring rush”.
blocks.46: At the start of the “herring season” in winter, boats came in to the steamer quay here with fresh herring. People used a lot of herring: it was salted in barrels as cured herring, smoked, dried, lightly salted and dried (nubbesild), boiled or fried fresh, made into herring cakes – all good food. When the first herring boat came, you could smell fried herring from every house in the whole area. Kristian Hanssen once wrote a long rhyme about this, I think it was during the war (40–45). Of it I can now remember only a few lines, which went roughly like this: “So they fried the herring, so the fat ran down, from Midtun at Hilla's, and Kamilla's ditto, all the way in to Flolid to Jakob's Nilla.” It may not be quite correctly reproduced, but it shows a little of the “feast” when the first load of herring came. Herring was important in the household, not least in the difficult war years.
blocks.47: There were few jobs for women here. The girls often worked as maids on the farms around, and for others who needed help. Many girls also went away and took jobs as housemaids, in shops and in hotels and cafés. Some trained as “seamstresses” and did sewing, either in sewing workshops or on their own. Gradually there were jobs in the sardine and herring oil factories that grew up, and in other factories that came along.
blocks.48: Little by little the administration of Gulen municipality was built up here, and in time it provided a good number of jobs for both women and men. The school has gradually been expanded and now employs 10–15 people (teachers, caretaker and cleaners). In 1959/60 came Gulen Gamleheim (old people's home), where several women got work. In 1975 the home was extended with a nursing home and was named Gulen Sjuke- og Aldersheim (nursing and old people's home), with even more jobs. Gulen Sanitetslag (the health association) was the developer, but when the home was finished it was taken over by the municipality. It was opened on 1 June 1975.
blocks.49: A few lines from the prologue at the handover ceremony:
blocks.50: Today we have hoisted our flags,
blocks.54: of our nursing home, beautiful and new,
blocks.55: finely placed in the shelter of the birch wood.
blocks.58: are glad of our nursing home,
blocks.59: and hope that the people for many, many years
blocks.60: will have much joy and benefit from it.
blocks.61: The health association, together with the district doctor Hallvard Natvik, was also behind the work of setting up Gulen dental clinic, which opened in the autumn of 1947. The first dentist was Reidar Tveit from Leikanger. He had partly grown up here, since his father, Olav Tveit, had earlier been a teacher in Eivindvik and parish clerk at Gulen church. The dental surgery was in the cellar of the bank building (the house Jørs now owns). Reidar Tveit left in 1951 and later became county dental officer in Sogn og Fjordane.
blocks.62: The first intake dam for Eivindvik waterworks..
blocks.63: Eivindvik waterworks was founded in 1955. The first dam (pictured) was built in Dalen above the parsonage. It was finished in 1957, but as more and more were connected to the network, the dam became too small. The old people's home and the school were big users of water, and in 1967–68 a small intake chamber was built in Kvernhuselva at Midtun, by Geitebykset, and a pipe laid up to it. A pipe was also laid from Svartevatnet over Svartevasshamrane. From there the water ran on in the river down to the intake at Geitebykset. In 1982 hoses were laid, over Gryta, all the way up to Svartevatnet, as we have it today. The waterworks was run as a jointly owned scheme, with joint efforts by the villagers, right up to 1 July 1992, when the municipality took over ownership and carried out a major expansion, including a modern treatment plant.
blocks.64: There is something I would like to include here, even though it has no direct connection with Eivindvik. It was Olai Blidensol (on Vassøy) who told me this. He worked at Johannes Steine's engineering workshop at Skjerjehamn. When they had nothing else to do, they used the time to make engines. I do not know whether the engines had a name, but in everyday speech they were called "Skjerjehamn engines". It was Steine who designed the engine, and in the workshop they made all the engine parts themselves, down to the smallest screw. In all 11 engines of about 5 hp were made. The first engine was sold to Søren Randal, who was then a teacher at Mjømna. The engine suited the boat it was in well and gave the boat good speed. I have heard that the "Skjerjehamn engines" were good and durable. Søren Randal came to Eivindvik as a teacher in 1946 and later became the first head of schools in Gulen. (His son Håkon Randal was also a trained teacher; he became a member of the Storting for Hordaland and later county governor there.)
blocks.66: When the tractor road in the valley was finished in 1981, a gathering was held at Ole-selet, attended by representatives of the agricultural authorities, both local and from the county, together with the landowners, the contractor Arne Eide and a number of other invited guests. The gathering was led by the chairman of the road committee, Rolf Midtun. Sour cream porridge and cured meats were served. Magnor Midtun read the following prologue:
blocks.69: The history of the dairy has proved difficult to trace. It has not been possible to find any of the minute books, either from the oldest dairy or from later times. The account books are also gone, but, as loose sheets, I have obtained a copy of the contract between the merchant Ola Midthun and Eivindvik Meierilag (the dairy cooperative) on renting premises in the cellar of his building (the contract is dated 20 September 1958), a copy of the articles of Eivindvik Meierilag “adopted at the founding meeting (annual meeting) in January 1959”, and extracts of accounts for the newly started dairy for the years 1959–1965, as well as accounts for the period 26 November–31 December 1958, construction accounts, drawn up by the bank cashier Konrad Elnes.
blocks.70: What I have written is therefore mostly based on oral information from people in the village. The most important informants are: Ivar Henriksbø, Harald Henriksbø, Ole J. Midtun, Hilda Brosvik, Odd Midttun and Rolf Midtun.
blocks.71: The local history of Gulen says that the first dairy in Gulen started at Undertun in 1893, but closed as early as 1895. From the information I have been given, Lars Underthun was heavily involved in founding it, and it was probably he who took the initiative.
blocks.72: The farmers delivered milk to the dairy, where it was separated, the cream churned, the butter made, packed and sent, probably to Bergen. The farmers took the skimmed milk and buttermilk home again, and it was used in the household and as animal feed. It was probably the farmers themselves who did the separating of the milk when they delivered it. At Undertun the dairy was most likely at farm no. 22, holding no. 3, where Lars lived.
blocks.73: Later, probably shortly after the closure at Undertun, the dairy was housed in “Hemingstova”, which stood where the community hall now stands. This house was named after a Heming Aritsson, who apparently came from Solund. He was church caretaker. The dairy built its own house at Gryta, right across the big river from Hemingstova, and a shoemaker, Hans Knutson Brandsdal, bought the house. He probably lived there for 10–15 years. Then he pulled the house down and moved to Litlebrandsdal, where it was put up again.
blocks.74: The dairy's name was, probably also when it was at Undertun, Midtunvågen Meieri. As far as I have been able to find, all joint ventures among the farmers here in older times had Midtunvågen in their name.
blocks.76: Hemingstova and the old dairy. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.77: In the picture the dairy building can just be made out in the middle. The light-coloured building on the far right is Hemingstova.
blocks.78: The dairy probably moved into the house at Gryta before 1900. The house was of wood with a concrete floor. Most of the people I have talked to could remember “the dairy site” as a concrete slab down by the river at farm no. 18, holding no. 3. From what people explain, the house must have been 7–8 m long and about 4 m wide, built in 1 ½ storeys. Just inside the front door there was a small passage where they set down the milk containers. Further on the ground floor there was a room for the dairy work and stairs up to the first floor, where the dairymaid lived. Ivar Henriksbø believed the dairymaid's kitchen was also on the ground floor. There was also space for storing ice. In “the ice house” the blocks of ice were kept in sawdust. They took the ice from the river, cutting out the blocks with large ice saws. Water was probably not piped in; they surely took water from the river that ran right past.
blocks.79: The separator, which some believe was an “Alfa Laval”, stood on a stand cast into the floor. A large barrel churn also stood on a stand. The separator and churn were driven by hand, and the farmers each had their days when they were to help with the separating. Here too they got skimmed milk and buttermilk to take home. The butter was made by the dairymaid, packed and sent to Bergen.
blocks.80: How long this old dairy at Gryta was in operation is not quite clear, but as the farmers bought separators themselves it became less needed. At any rate it seems to have closed before 1919, for then the materials from the house are said to have been used in extending the house at farm no. 21, holding no. 7, belonging to Jon Henriksbø, who bought the dairy house. The separator was bought by Hans Undertun, it is said. Perhaps the dairy closed during the First World War. The old dairy was an institution in the village. People met there, talked and heard the news; it was a gathering place of great social value.
blocks.81: Some years later, after the village road came (1924), an attempt was made to deliver milk to Høyanger. A room for receiving it was arranged in Sheriff Bredvik's boathouse. Betzy Larsen (Hummelsund) was employed to do the weighing. A well was made above the boathouse and a cooling tank inside it. This arrangement started one autumn and lasted about 1 ½ years. Then it stopped because the milk buyers in Høyanger did not pay. Some of the farmers here lost money on this arrangement.
blocks.83: After this the farmers churned their own butter and sold it to the merchants. But the need for better and more secure sale of the butter made itself felt, and (probably in the mid-1930s) a butter cooperative was started to get firmer and more stable reception in Bergen. By agreement with the firm P.R. Sandal, a butter kneader was bought and placed in Sandal's private house. The farmers churned the butter themselves and delivered it on fixed days to Sandal's, where the butter was kneaded, packed and sent to Bergen. During the war of 1940–45 the farmers were required to deliver butter, as other farm produce, with a certain quantity from each holding, according to its size.
blocks.84: Around 1950 the butter reception was moved to the merchant Ola Midthun. For a time the kneader then stood in the community hall. Later it was moved to the cellar of Haldis and Arne Fosse's house; they did the kneading and packing of the butter.
blocks.85: The butter cooperatives were an arrangement for those who did not deliver milk to a dairy, and gradually some farmers who lived outside Eivindvik also joined the butter cooperative here. Thus Brandsdal, Glosvik, Undalsvik, Klokeid, Neverdal, Hausevik (Vesetvik), Hisarøy and the area along Strendene delivered butter here. Later some farmers in Austgulfjorden who did not deliver milk joined this cooperative. Some of the farmers at Grinde also delivered butter here at times.
blocks.86: The butter cooperative was called, at least towards the end, Eivindvik Smørlag, and the arrangement lasted right up until Eivindvik Meieri started on 1 December 1958.
blocks.87: Without having prices and statistics to point to, we must believe that the old dairy and butter cooperative arrangements meant a great deal in enabling the farmers to sell their produce in a good and practical way and at the best prices obtainable on the market at various times.
blocks.89: When the new dairy started, the butter reception did not end after all. The dairy cooperative's accounts for 1959 to 1962 show that butter was also received through the butter cooperative in these years, probably from those who lived outside Eivindvik and could not deliver milk. But here in the village separating and churning came to an end then. The milk was delivered to the dairy and weighed there, and what was not sold locally was sent to the Bergen dairy on the passenger boats. Transport to the local dairy was arranged by the individual farmers taking turns to drive the milk to the dairy. The empty churns were taken back. Each holding also had its fixed days for driving the milk from the dairy to the steamer quay for dispatch to the Bergen dairy. The dairy was in the cellar under the shop in Ola Midthun's house the whole time. It was fitted out with a modern cooling tank there. Haldis and Arne Fosse did the weighing. The contract between the merchant Ola Midthun and Eivindvik Meierilag concerning the letting of premises to Eivindvik Meieri is, as mentioned, dated 20 September 1958 and was to apply from the day the dairy started operating. The rent was set at 25 kroner a month.
blocks.90: The dairy was also to be able to use the freezer unit installed (Ola Midthun was also renting out freezer compartments at that time) to run the cooling tank machinery, “for rent at the usual rates”.
blocks.91: The articles of the dairy cooperative were to be adopted at the “founding meeting (annual meeting) in January 1959”. The copy of the articles I have seen is an unsigned copy, but there is reason to believe it contains the text as correctly adopted. Article 1 reads:
blocks.92: “S/L Eivindvik Meierilag is a cooperative of farmers in Eivindvik and the immediate surroundings. It is a shareholders' cooperative with limited liability and variable membership and capital.
blocks.93: It has its head office in Eivindvik in Gulen municipality.”
blocks.94: Article 2 goes on to say that the purpose of the cooperative is “dairy operation and the sale of milk and milk products”.
blocks.95: The articles also lay down that “the cooperative's capital consists of shares of 25 kroner – twenty-five kroner – per cow”, and that one share was to be subscribed “for each dairy cow that the farm with reasonable management feeds from year to year.” It was further decided that for shares subscribed, “security shall be given that the dairy cooperative can use as security for loans. (Share loans.)” It also appears that the shares are to follow the farm, and article 4 says, among other things: “The shares may not be transferred by anyone by purchase, inheritance, gift, pledge or debt collection without the consent of the annual meeting.”
blocks.96: Article 6 lays down the obligation to deliver; it says among other things: “Each shareholder has the right and the duty to deliver all the milk the farm produces, except what is used on the farm or sold to people who live permanently or work on the farm”. The articles fill 4 full A4 pages and are quite detailed.
blocks.97: The construction accounts show a total cost of 4,728.05 kroner.
blocks.98: The members of the dairy cooperative: Ivar Henriksbø 6 shares, Jakob Hauge 6 shares, Ole J. Midtun 6 shares, Edvard Fosse 3 shares, Asbjørn Underthun 5 shares, Rolf Midtun 6 shares, Gerhard Wergeland 4 shares, Harald Eide 1 share, Odd Midttun 5 shares, Konrad Elnes 3 shares, Harald Nese 4 shares, Harald Henriksbø 3 shares, Olav Undertun 2 shares, Erling Oppedal 3 shares, Herman Henriksbø 2 shares, Torleif Henriksbø 2 shares, Ingvald Sognefest 3 shares and Nils Navdal 3 shares.
blocks.100: In the first year of operation, 1959, the accounts show that a total of 144,130.2 kg of milk was weighed in. Local sales amounted to 22,213.5 litres, and the rest, 117,895 litres, was sent to the Bergen dairy.
blocks.101: “The average price paid to producers is 67.23 øre for 3.75% fat”, it says in the accounts. The total paid to suppliers was 93,881.61 kroner. The same year butter was sold for 113,533.60 kroner.
blocks.102: The following year, 1960, a total of 176,118.8 kg was weighed in, converted to 171,360 litres. Of this, 23,097 litres were sold locally. The average price paid was 68.3 øre per kg, the gross payment to suppliers 124,395.40 kroner in all. Butter sales were 119,279.33 kroner.
blocks.103: According to the copies of accounts I have seen, 1963 shows the highest figure for milk weighed in, at 197,240 kg. That year has no figure for butter deliveries. The reason is that from that year on, the butter cooperative's accounts were separated from the dairy accounts.
blocks.104: The largest local sales are shown in the accounts for 1964, at 35,898 litres, but this figure is fairly steady in the last three years for which I have seen copies of the accounts (63–64–65), at over 35,000 litres each year. The average fat content was 3.9% in all these 3 years. The average price to producers was highest in 1965, at 87 øre per litre.
blocks.105: Eivindvik Meieri was in full operation until deliveries were arranged to a collection station for the Bergen dairy at Duesund. That happened in 1967. The milk was then collected by lorry from each holding. The milk lorry's first trip here was on 1 April 1967. That day it snowed, and the lorry could not make it up to Midtun. The haulier demanded that the road be put in order, and while the improvement work went on, the people at Midtun had to drive the milk down to Grytekroken.
blocks.106: At first the milk was also carried in churns on the milk lorry; later they went over to tankers, and gradually the farmers had milking installations with tanks put into their farm buildings.
blocks.107: Since the minute books of both the butter and milk dairies have not been traced, I can say little about who led the business over the years. At the start of the first butter dairy, which came in 1893, it seems, as mentioned, that Lars Underthun played a large part.
blocks.108: The chairmen of the last dairy from 1958 onwards were:
blocks.109: 1958 Asbjørn Underthun 1959 Odd Midttun 1960–62 Rolf Midtun 1963–67 Ivar Henriksbø
blocks.110: The accountant in all these years was the merchant Ola Midthun, who also handled what remained of the butter cooperative's business.
blocks.111: It seems that the organisation was called Eivindvik Meierilag, but that the business itself used the name Eivindvik Meieri. This name is used, among other places, in the copy I have seen of the rental contract of 20 September 1958, and was also used in everyday speech.
blocks.112: The annual meetings of the dairy cooperative seem to have been arranged almost as parties, with good food (sour cream porridge etc.), talks, readings, song and music and various other entertainment.
blocks.113: In 1967 everything to do with dairy operation in Eivindvik came to an end. An era in the village's economic life was over; indeed, we may also say that part of the social life of the village disappeared. The many pleasant trips with the milk churns and the cosy conversations at the dairy had become history. The good memories of a toilsome but good and happy time must be allowed to live.
blocks.114: Breeding good animals was closely connected with milk and butter production. Several arrangements for promoting milk, meat and other agricultural production came about in our village in the same period as the dairy cooperation. Such arrangements were Midtunvågen fealslag (cattle breeding association), Midtunvågen sauealslag (sheep breeding association), Midtunvågen slaktelag (slaughter cooperative) and Midtunvågen jordbrukslag (farming cooperative). The farming cooperative closed, and then came Eivindvik innkjøpslag (purchasing cooperative), which is still in operation.
blocks.115: The slaughter cooperative was a member of Vestlandske Salslag and disappeared when the farmers began delivering their animals for slaughter alive to the cooperative. The tasks of the cattle breeding association were taken over by the dairy cooperative in the 1960s.
blocks.116: In 1929 the cattle breeding association set up the arrangement with breeding bulls. Ivar Henriksbø has told this; he kept the bulls from 1935 until the arrangement ended in 1965. The bulls were surely not always easy to handle. I remember that they sometimes turned vicious, and then it could be no joke to deal with the big, powerful animals. But it went well.
blocks.117: I do not know when the cattle breeding association and the other associations were started, nor how and by whom they were organised, but since there was a certain connection between all the associations the farmers formed to promote and develop agriculture and secure firmer and better sales of their produce, I wanted to mention here those of them I know have existed in the village. It shows that the farmers were very much part of developing society and that they were concerned with improving conditions for the people who lived here. By taking part in the joint ventures, people enjoyed the benefits these ventures created, both directly in kroner and øre and indirectly through the new ideas, well-being and comfort they brought.
